In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of new methods for the study of the sorption of organic chemicals by soil.
the effects of soil solution chemistry and ionic strength on the adsorption and desorption of pesticides in soil.
the sorption and desorption of the herbicides bromacil, diuron, norflurazone, and simazine in a Candler fine-sand soil.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sorption/desorptions of bromacil and diuron are influenced by the ionic strength and the cation composition of the electrolyte, but the influence of these electrolyte factors on the sorption/desorptlon of simazine and norflurazon is negligible.
the presence of Ca2+ ions in the soil solution, as well as the ionic strength of that solution, can influence the sorption/desorp- tion of herbicides in soils.
the presence of electrolyte ions in the soil solution, especially Ca2+, can enhance sorption of pesticides to soil.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
soil sorption of herbicides is affected by electrolyte cation composition as well as by ionic strength.

the use of ionic strength as a parameter to predict the sorption of pesticides by soils may be limited to the use of a single electrolyte, and may not be applicable to soils with a large amount of organic matter.
the presence of organic matter in soils increases the retention of pesticides in soil.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have developed a new method to measure the rate of sorption and desorption of pesticides from soils.
the presence of a soil organic carbon (SOC) fraction with a higher aromaticity than the bulk SOC is a key factor in the sorption of the herbicides studied.

the use of a cation exchange resin to remove divalent cations from the solution can be a useful tool to improve the accuracy of sorption measurements in the absence of an ion-exchange reaction between the soil and the cations in the solution.
